cards.q: Why does println! have an exclamation mark?
cards.a: It is a macro, which lets it take a format string and any number of arguments checked at compile time.
cards.lessonTitle: Rust and Cargo: Your First Program

cards.q: What does cargo check do?
cards.a: It type-checks the project without producing a program, which is faster than a full build.
cards.lessonTitle: Rust and Cargo: Your First Program

cards.q: What is the difference between shadowing and mut?
cards.a: mut lets one variable change; shadowing declares a new variable with the same name, which may have a different type.

cards.q: Why does let y: i64 = x; not compile when x is an i32?
cards.a: Rust never converts numeric types implicitly; write x.into() or i64::from(x).

cards.q: What does a function return if its body's last line is x * x; with a semicolon?
cards.a: () (unit), which causes a type error if the function declares another return type.

cards.q: Can if be used on the right of a let?
cards.a: Yes: if is an expression, so let s = if c { a } else { b }; works (both branches must have the same type).

cards.q: How can a loop produce a value?
cards.a: break value; inside a loop makes the whole loop expression evaluate to value.

cards.q: What does 1..=5 include?
cards.a: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5; 1..5 would exclude 5.

cards.q: Which parameter type should a function that only reads text use?
cards.a: &str, so it accepts string literals and borrowed Strings alike.

cards.q: Why must you trim the result of read_line before parsing it?
cards.a: read_line keeps the line break, and "42\n" does not parse as a number.

cards.q: When is a String's heap memory freed?
cards.a: When its owner goes out of scope (it is dropped), unless ownership was moved elsewhere first.

cards.q: Why can you still use a after let b = a; when a is an i32 but not when it is a String?
cards.a: i32 is Copy, so assignment copies it; String owns heap data, so assignment moves it.

cards.q: Why can't you hold &v[0] while calling v.push(4)?
cards.a: push may reallocate the vector, which would leave the shared reference pointing at freed memory; the borrow rules forbid a mutable borrow while a shared one is alive.

cards.q: How do you change an i32 through an &mut i32 parameter n?
cards.a: Dereference it: *n += 1.

cards.q: Why should a function that sums numbers take &[i32] instead of &Vec<i32>?
cards.a: A slice accepts arrays, vectors and parts of either; &Vec only accepts whole vectors.

cards.q: What does &s[0..3] contain for s = "hello"?
cards.a: "hel": bytes 0, 1 and 2.

cards.q: What is the difference between &self and &mut self in a method?
cards.a: &self only borrows the value to read it; &mut self borrows it mutably so the method can change fields.

cards.q: How is an associated function such as new called?
cards.a: With the type name and ::, for example Counter::new("clicks").

cards.q: Why is Option<T> safer than null?
cards.a: The type says the value may be missing, and the compiler makes you handle None before using the value.

cards.q: What does ? do on an Option inside a function returning Option?
cards.a: Unwraps Some(v) to v, or returns None from the function immediately.

cards.q: What is the difference between v[5] and v.get(5) when v has 3 items?
cards.a: v[5] panics; v.get(5) returns None.

cards.q: What happens to a vector after for x in v { }?
cards.a: It is moved into the loop and consumed; iterate over &v to keep it.

cards.q: Why does "é".len() return 2?
cards.a: len counts bytes, and é takes two bytes in UTF-8.

cards.q: How do you get each character together with the byte position where it starts?
cards.a: s.char_indices().

cards.q: What does *counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1 do?
cards.a: Inserts 0 for a new word, then adds 1 to the stored count either way.

cards.q: When should you choose BTreeMap over HashMap?
cards.a: When you need the keys in sorted order, ranges of keys, or the smallest/largest key.

cards.q: What does the ? operator do with an Err value?
cards.a: Returns it from the current function immediately (converting it with From if needed).

cards.q: When is panicking the right choice instead of returning a Result?
cards.a: For bugs and broken invariants that the caller cannot sensibly handle, not for expected failures like bad input.

cards.q: Can code outside a module call a function in it that is not marked pub?
cards.a: No: items are private to their module (and its children) unless marked pub.

cards.q: Why do unit tests live in a mod tests with #[cfg(test)]?
cards.a: The module is compiled only when running tests, and as a child module it can reach private items with use super::*.

cards.q: Why does fn largest<T>(items: &[T]) -> T need a bound such as PartialOrd?
cards.a: Without a bound the compiler knows nothing about T, so the body could not compare items with >.

cards.q: What does impl Pair<f64> { ... } mean?
cards.a: Those methods exist only for Pair<f64>, not for other Pair types.

cards.q: What is a default method in a trait?
cards.a: A method with a body in the trait; implementers get it for free and may override it.

cards.q: Why can't you implement std::fmt::Display for Vec<i32>?
cards.a: The orphan rule: neither the trait nor the type belongs to your crate.

cards.q: Why can't f64 implement Eq and Ord?
cards.a: NaN is not equal to itself and is not ordered, so equality and ordering are only partial.

cards.q: What do you get for free by implementing From<A> for B?
cards.a: Into<B> for A, so a.into() produces a B.

cards.q: What does fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str promise?
cards.a: The returned reference is valid as long as both inputs are, so it may borrow from either.

cards.q: Why does fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str need no lifetime annotation?
cards.a: With one input reference, elision gives the output the same lifetime.

cards.q: Why must a dyn Trait value sit behind a pointer such as Box or &?
cards.a: Its concrete type, and therefore its size, is not known at compile time.

cards.q: When is an enum better than Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>?
cards.a: When the set of variants is fixed and known: matching is simpler, checked for completeness and has no vtable.

cards.q: What does move change about a closure?
cards.a: It captures the variables it uses by value (taking ownership) instead of by reference.

cards.q: Which bound should a function use if it calls the closure many times and the closure may change its captures?
cards.a: FnMut.

cards.q: Why does (1..).map(|n| n * n) not run forever?
cards.a: Adapters are lazy: nothing is computed until a consumer such as take(5).collect() asks for values.

cards.q: What does collecting an iterator of Result<T, E> into Result<Vec<T>, E> do?
cards.a: Gives Ok with all values, or the first Err, stopping there.

cards.q: What must you write to implement Iterator for your type?
cards.a: The associated type Item and the method next; all other iterator methods are provided.

cards.q: Why does Words<'a> need a lifetime?
cards.a: Its items are slices borrowed from the original text, which must outlive them.

cards.q: Why does a recursive enum like List need Box?
cards.a: Without a pointer, the type would contain itself and have infinite size; a Box has a fixed size.

cards.q: What happens if you call borrow_mut() on a RefCell that is already borrowed?
cards.a: It panics at run time, because RefCell checks the borrowing rules while the program runs.

cards.q: What does c @ 'a'..='z' do in a match arm?
cards.a: Matches a char in that range and binds the matched value to c.

cards.q: Why can't you write let Some(x) = maybe_value; without else?
cards.a: Some(x) is refutable: let needs a pattern that always matches, or an else branch for when it does not.

cards.q: Why does thread::spawn usually need a move closure?
cards.a: The thread may outlive the current function, so it must own its data rather than borrow local variables.

cards.q: When does iterating over an mpsc receiver end?
cards.a: When every sender has been dropped and the channel is empty.

cards.q: Why is the data inside the Mutex rather than next to it?
cards.a: So the only way to reach it is through lock(), which makes unsynchronised access impossible to write.
cards.lessonTitle: Shared State with Arc and Mutex

cards.q: What is the thread-safe version of Rc<RefCell<T>>?
cards.a: Arc<Mutex<T>> (or Arc<RwLock<T>>).
cards.lessonTitle: Shared State with Arc and Mutex

cards.q: What does calling an async fn return?
cards.a: A future, which does nothing until it is awaited or spawned on a runtime.

cards.q: Why is calling std::thread::sleep inside an async task a problem?
cards.a: It blocks the runtime's thread, stopping every other task scheduled on it; use the async sleep instead.

cards.q: What are documentation tests?
cards.a: Code examples inside /// comments that cargo test compiles and runs, so the examples stay correct.

cards.q: Why measure performance only with --release builds?
cards.a: Debug builds are unoptimised and include extra checks, so they can be many times slower.

cards.q: Why should main stay small in a CLI program?
cards.a: So the logic lives in testable functions that return Results, and only main decides how to print errors and which exit code to use.

cards.q: Why read standard input when no file path is given?
cards.a: The tool can then be used in pipelines, receiving data from another program.

cards.q: Why does `square!(2 + 3)` give 25?
cards.a: The `expr` fragment keeps `2 + 3` as one expression, so the expansion behaves like `(2 + 3) * (2 + 3)`.

cards.q: What does `$( ... ),*` mean in a macro pattern?
cards.a: The part in brackets may appear any number of times, separated by commas.

cards.q: Why take `&str` rather than `&String` as a parameter?
cards.a: Deref coercion turns `&String` (and `&Box<String>`) into `&str`, so a `&str` parameter accepts every kind of string; `&String` accepts only one.

cards.q: When does `Cow` save work?
cards.a: When a function usually returns its input unchanged: it hands back the borrowed input instead of allocating a copy.

cards.q: Does `unsafe` turn off the borrow checker?
cards.a: No. It allows five extra operations; every other check still applies.

cards.q: Why is calling a C function always unsafe?
cards.a: The compiler cannot see inside it, so it cannot check that the call respects memory safety; the programmer must promise it does.

cards.q: When should you use `BufReader` instead of `read_to_string`?
cards.a: When the file may be large: it reads a piece at a time instead of loading the whole file into memory.

cards.q: Why pass arguments to `Command` as a list?
cards.a: Each argument stays one argument whatever characters it contains; nothing is interpreted by a shell.

cards.q: Why do the transition methods take `self` and not `&mut self`?
cards.a: Taking ownership moves the value, so the old state cannot be used after the transition; the compiler enforces it.

cards.q: What does `PhantomData<T>` cost at run time?
cards.a: Nothing: it has size zero. It only tells the compiler the type uses `T`.
